We have already seen some properties of matrix multiplication. For example, multiplying any [MATH: n \times n] square matrix [MATH: A] by the identity matrix [MATH: I_n] will leave it unchanged:
[MATH: A I_n = I_n A = A.]
Also, matrix multiplication follows the distributive laws:
[MATH: (A + B)C|= AC + BC,; C(A + B)|= CA + CB.]

items.title: Calculating a Matrix Product Using the Distributive Law

sections.normalized_html:
We can apply the distributive law

[MATH: AB-CB=(A-C)B.]

So, we calculate [MATH: A-C] first:

[MATH: A − C|= [2|4|− 3; − 1|− 5|3; − 2|0|7] − [3|4|− 3; − 1|− 4|3; − 2|0|8]; = [− 1|0|0; 0|− 1|0; 0|0|− 1]; = − I_{3}]

Finally, we obtain

[MATH: AB − CB|= (A − C)B; = − I_{3}B; = − B; = [− sqrt(2)|− sqrt(3)|45; − 81|sqrt(5)|2; − 2|− 1|− sqrt(3)].]

If [MATH: A,] [MATH: B,] and [MATH: C] are three matrices that are conformable for multiplication, then they follow the associative law:
[MATH: \left( AB\right) C = A\left( BC\right)]

Content:
So, when we wish to compute a product [MATH: ABC,] we don't always have to start by multiplying [MATH: AB.] Alternatively, we can start by multiplying [MATH: BC,] and then multiply [MATH: A] by the result.

Content:
Sometimes rearranging the parentheses might make the computations slightly easier.

items.title: Calculating a Matrix Product Using the Associative Law

sections.normalized_html:
First, recall the associative law

[MATH: ABC = (AB)C = A(BC).]

Notice that [MATH: A] is a [MATH: 3 \times 3] matrix, [MATH: B] is a [MATH: 3 \times 3] matrix, and [MATH: C] is a [MATH: 3 \times 1] matrix. Therefore,

  • multiplying [MATH: A] by [MATH: B], we will obtain a [MATH: 3 \times 3] matrix that will require finding [MATH: 9] entries, while

  • multiplying [MATH: B] by [MATH: C], we will obtain a [MATH: 3 \times 1] matrix that will require finding only [MATH: 3] entries.

So, we find the product [MATH: BC] first:

[MATH: BC|= [− 2|5|− 4; 2|1|1; − 4|3|− 1] ⋅ [− 2; 1; 3]; = [− 3; 0; 8]]

Now, we multiply [MATH: A] by [MATH: BC\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: ABC|= A(BC); = [1|− 1|0; 4|3|1; 1|2|1] ⋅ [− 3; 0; 8]; = [− 3; − 4; 5]]

items.title: Identifying True Statements Regarding Matrix Multiplication

sections.normalized_html:
Given that [MATH: A, B,] and [MATH: C] are [MATH: 6 \times 6] matrices, which of the following statements are always true?

  1. [MATH: A(BC) = (AB)C]

  2. [MATH: A(B+C) = BA+CA]

  3. [MATH: A(B+C) = AB+AC]

Given that [MATH: A, B,] and [MATH: C] are [MATH: 6 \times 6] matrices, which of the following statements are always true?

1. [MATH: A(BC) = (AB)C]
2. [MATH: A(B+C) = BA+CA]
3. [MATH: A(B+C) = AB+AC]

sections.normalized_html:
Let's consider the statements one by one.

  • Statement I is true. Matrix multiplication is associative, so [MATH: (AB)C = A(BC)] in general.

  • Statement II is false. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so [MATH: A(B+C) = AB + AC] in general. However, since matrix multiplication is not commutative, we have [MATH: AB + AC \neq BA + CA.]

  • Statement III is true. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so [MATH: (A+B)C = AC+BC,] and [MATH: A(B+C) = AB+AC] in general.

Therefore, only statements I and III are true.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We have already seen some properties of matrix multiplication. For example, multiplying any [MATH: n \times n] square matrix [MATH: A] by the identity matrix [MATH: I_n] will leave it unchanged:
[MATH: A I_n = I_n A = A.]
Also, matrix multiplication follows the distributive laws:
[MATH: (A + B)C|= AC + BC,; C(A + B)|= CA + CB.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating a Matrix Product Using the Distributive Law

Example Prompt:
Find [MATH: AB-CB,] where
[MATH: [2|4|− 3; − 1|− 5|3; − 2|0|7]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We can apply the distributive law

[MATH: AB-CB=(A-C)B.]

So, we calculate [MATH: A-C] first:

[MATH: A − C|= [2|4|− 3; − 1|− 5|3; − 2|0|7] − [3|4|− 3; − 1|− 4|3; − 2|0|8]; = [− 1|0|0; 0|− 1|0; 0|0|− 1]; = − I_{3}]

Finally, we obtain

[MATH: AB − CB|= (A − C)B; = − I_{3}B; = − B; = [− sqrt(2)|− sqrt(3)|45; − 81|sqrt(5)|2; − 2|− 1|− sqrt(3)].]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Associative Law for Matrix Multiplication

Content:
If [MATH: A,] [MATH: B,] and [MATH: C] are three matrices that are conformable for multiplication, then they follow the associative law:
[MATH: \left( AB\right) C = A\left( BC\right)]

Content:
So, when we wish to compute a product [MATH: ABC,] we don't always have to start by multiplying [MATH: AB.] Alternatively, we can start by multiplying [MATH: BC,] and then multiply [MATH: A] by the result.

Content:
Sometimes rearranging the parentheses might make the computations slightly easier.

Explanation:
First, recall the associative law

[MATH: ABC = (AB)C = A(BC).]

Notice that [MATH: A] is a [MATH: 3 \times 3] matrix, [MATH: B] is a [MATH: 3 \times 3] matrix, and [MATH: C] is a [MATH: 3 \times 1] matrix. Therefore,

- multiplying [MATH: A] by [MATH: B], we will obtain a [MATH: 3 \times 3] matrix that will require finding [MATH: 9] entries, while
- multiplying [MATH: B] by [MATH: C], we will obtain a [MATH: 3 \times 1] matrix that will require finding only [MATH: 3] entries.

So, we find the product [MATH: BC] first:

[MATH: BC|= [− 2|5|− 4; 2|1|1; − 4|3|− 1] ⋅ [− 2; 1; 3]; = [− 3; 0; 8]]

Now, we multiply [MATH: A] by [MATH: BC\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: ABC|= A(BC); = [1|− 1|0; 4|3|1; 1|2|1] ⋅ [− 3; 0; 8]; = [− 3; − 4; 5]]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Matrix Multiplication Is Not Commutative in General

Content:
In general, matrix multiplication is not commutative. In other words, given two general matrices [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] that are conformable for multiplication, we have
[MATH: AB \neq BA.]

Content:
However, some particular matrices may satisfy this property. For instance, [MATH: AI = IA] (where [MATH: I] is the identity matrix).

Item 10 — Example: Identifying True Statements Regarding Matrix Multiplication

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: A, B,] and [MATH: C] are [MATH: 6 \times 6] matrices, which of the following statements are always true?

1. [MATH: A(BC) = (AB)C]
2. [MATH: A(B+C) = BA+CA]
3. [MATH: A(B+C) = AB+AC]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's consider the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. Matrix multiplication is associative, so [MATH: (AB)C = A(BC)] in general.
- Statement II is false. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so [MATH: A(B+C) = AB + AC] in general. However, since matrix multiplication is not commutative, we have
[MATH: AB + AC \neq BA + CA.]
- Statement III is true. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so [MATH: (A+B)C = AC+BC,] and [MATH: A(B+C) = AB+AC] in general.

Therefore, only statements I and III are true.
